insights:
## Consistency

Training days per week moved from **3.3 over the last 13 weeks to 4.2 over the last 4 weeks**, and this week itself shows **5 training days against 6 the prior week** — a small pullback but still part of a pattern that's trending up over the last month. The last 90 days show **43 active training days**, averaging a session every **2 days**. This week's discipline mix (3 running, 1 cycling, 1 strength, 1 yoga) also broadened out from last week's strength-heavy split (3 strength, 2 running, 1 cycling, 1 yoga), suggesting the week-to-week mix is rotating rather than locking into a single pattern.

## Running

Running has picked up recently — **9 sessions in the last 30 days** versus 15 for the full last 90, meaning more than half of the last quarter's running volume landed in the most recent month. That said, average pace slowed from **10:21/mi in the first half of the year to 13:36/mi in the second half**. Without incline or distance data for context, this is hard to read as a fitness change on its own — it may reflect a shift toward easier-effort runs, which lines up with the average heart rate of **155.8 bpm** across the last 90 days of running, a moderate-to-high aerobic zone for a 20-25 minute effort.

On form, cadence held essentially flat at **168.1 spm in the first half versus 166.9 spm in the second half** — both comfortably above the 165 spm efficiency benchmark, so turnover rate isn't drifting. Vertical oscillation and ground contact time both increased slightly (oscillation **7.9 → 8.3 cm**, GCT **253 → 261.7 ms**), moving further from the 7.5 cm and 260 ms benchmarks. Since cadence stayed steady while oscillation and GCT rose, the extra time in contact with the ground isn't coming from slower steps — it reads more like reduced spring off the ground in the second half. One cue worth trying: focus on quick, light steps off the ground on a few runs, almost like the ground is warm — that directly targets GCT without needing to change cadence, which is already in a good place.

## Strength

Strength training shows **16 sessions over the last year**, with Hip Thrust (11 sessions), Shoulder Press (11), and Lunge (10) as the most consistent lifters. Average loads across the board — mid-20s to mid-30s lbs — are close together across different movement patterns (squat, deadlift, press, curl), which is typical of a Peloton movement-tracker dataset rather than a free-weight progressive-overload program. The last 30 days show **6 strength sessions**, roughly on par with the 90-day rate of ~1.3/week, so this isn't a discipline that's been neglected — it's held steady alongside the running increase.

## Recovery and Training Load

Training load jumped from **371.5 (prior 7 days) to 413.5 (last 7 days)**, a real increase tied directly to the uptick in training days. Recovery signals over the same window are mixed rather than uniformly moving one direction: **HRV improved slightly (46.7 → 48.0 ms)** and **body battery at wake rose (81.5 → 87.1)**, but **sleep score dropped (75.0 → 72.4)** and **readiness score declined (76.4 → 71.9)**. Garmin's own status reads **"Recovery,"** which together with the readiness dip suggests the recent volume increase is registering as fresh stress rather than something fully absorbed yet — worth watching over the next week or two rather than pushing training days higher immediately.

## Nutrition

Protein intake is close to target: **132.6g average against a 140g goal**, with **19 of 28 logged days hitting the protein target** — a reasonable fueling base for a week that includes 6 strength sessions. Calories are landing under target more often than not (**1483 avg vs. 1650 target, only 20/28 days hit**), which combined with rising training load and declining readiness is a combination worth noting — under-fueling relative to target during a volume increase is one of the more common contributors to the kind of readiness dip showing up this week. Fiber is the furthest from target (**21.6g vs. 25g, 15/28 days hit**) but logging consistency itself — **28 of 30 days tracked** — is a dependable base to build any of these adjustments on top of.

intervention_analysis.text:
## Headline
The step up to 1mg semaglutide over the past four weeks coincided with meaningful body composition improvements — fat mass down 5.1% (46.92→44.52 lb) and weight down 0.8% — alongside better sleep and training readiness, but this came with a slight uptick in physiological stress markers (resting HR, HRV, Body Battery High all moved in the "worsened" direction), suggesting the body is still adapting to the dose increase.

## What the data suggests
The body composition changes are the standout finding and align well with semaglutide's known mechanism: fat mass dropped 5.1% while muscle mass actually increased 0.9% (107.04→107.95 lb), a favorable pattern likely helped by concurrent creatine supplementation supporting lean mass retention during a caloric deficit. Average daily intake of 1514 kcal with 135g protein (about 0.8g/lb bodyweight) is consistent with appetite suppression plus a protein-forward eating pattern conducive to preserving muscle while losing fat. Training readiness rose 7.2% and sleep score improved 3.8%, with deep sleep up 4.2% — all positive signs that the body is recovering reasonably well despite the deficit.

The countervailing signal is a cluster of autonomic/recovery metrics moving slightly negative: resting HR up 1.5%, HRV down 2.0% (nightly) and 0.4% (weekly), Body Battery High down 3.9%, and stress average up 1.3%. These are small magnitude shifts, but their consistency suggests mild additional physiological load, plausibly from the dose increase itself (GI/appetite effects, lower intake, or the metabolic adjustment period common in the first weeks after a semaglutide titration step) rather than random noise. This pattern — good sleep architecture and readiness scores but slightly elevated resting HR/stress and depressed HRV — is a classic "body adapting to a new stressor" signature rather than a red flag, but it's worth monitoring rather than dismissing.

Nutrition comparisons before/after cannot be treated as a true intervention effect here, since the before window had 0% logging coverage. The after-window macros are informative as a standalone snapshot (1514 kcal, 135g protein, 141g carbs, 44g fat, 22g fiber) but say nothing about what changed, since there's no baseline to compare against.

## Caveats and confounds
This is a single-subject, non-blinded, short observation window (28 days each side) with multiple concurrent interventions — creatine monohydrate started on the same day as the "before" window began, and semaglutide itself was already active at 0.5mg before the dose increase, meaning the "after" period reflects a dose escalation on top of ~8 weeks of existing drug exposure rather than a true drug-naive comparison. The 0% nutrition logging in the before window makes any food-related before/after claims unreliable; the after-window figures are only useful as absolute reference points. Natural week-to-week variation in HRV and resting HR (typically 3-5%) means the small worsening in those metrics may fall within normal noise rather than reflecting a genuine physiological cost of the dose increase. Seasonal/behavioral factors (e.g., increased step count, 9002→9450) could also be influencing recovery metrics independently of the medication.

## What to watch next
- Track whether resting HR and HRV continue trending adversely over the next 2-4 weeks — if they stabilize or reverse, this likely was a transient adaptation to the dose increase rather than a lasting cost.
- Watch protein intake relative to the continuing weight loss trajectory (currently 135g/day) to ensure muscle mass gains hold as fat loss continues at 1mg.
- Monitor Body Battery High and stress average specifically, since they're the most consistent "worsened" signals — if they continue declining alongside readiness/sleep still improving, that divergence is worth flagging to a clinician monitoring the titration.

nutrition_insights.text:
## What's working

Calories hit target on **28 of 28 logged days**, with a 30-day average of **1,483 kcal** against a 1,650 target. Weight moved from **168.5lb to 167.6lb (-0.9lb)** over the same window, consistent with the calorie pattern. Protein logging also shows a repeatable base: cottage cheese, oatmeal, protein powder, banana, and salmon each logged **13-16 times** in 30 days, with salmon fillet averaging **40g protein** per entry — a reliable anchor for hitting the 140g target.

## Where the friction is

Protein target was hit **19 of 28 days** (68%), and the weekday/weekend split shows why: weekday protein averages **127g** vs **146g** on weekends, a 19g gap. Fiber tracks a similar pattern — **21g weekdays vs 24g weekends**, both under the 25g target, with the 30-day average landing at **22g** and hitting target only **15 of 28 days**. The weekday dip in both metrics suggests whatever's different about weekday logging (fewer meals, smaller portions, or just less variety) is the harder window to manage.

## Specific suggestions

Since protein powder is already logged **15 times** at 25g each and cottage cheese **16 times** at 12g each, adding one more serving of either on weekdays specifically would likely close most of the 19g weekday protein gap without introducing a new food. For fiber, the gap to target is small (**22g avg vs 25g target** — just 3g short), so something like adding the banana you're already eating 15x/month to a weekday slot where it's currently missing could close it without meal-prep overhead. No need to overhaul weekend eating — it's already closer to target on both metrics.

## Watch list

The 1mg semaglutide dose started **33 days ago (week 5)** — worth watching whether calorie intake drifts lower from the current 1,483 average, since appetite reduction is an expected effect at higher doses for some people. With a 5K goal added to two strength days, keep an eye on whether 1,483 kcal and 133g protein stay sufficient as running volume increases.

pattern_insights:
## This week's recovery picture looks like overreaching, not illness
**What the data shows:** Earlier this week shows sleep score cratering to 65 (down from 79 the prior week — the best of the whole 60 days) while body battery peak simultaneously spiked to 95 (the highest in the dataset) and readiness dropped to 66. This is the same combination seen two weeks ago (sleep 73, body battery 89, readiness 66) — both coincide with workout-volume spikes the week before (7 workouts three weeks ago, 6 workouts two weeks ago) right before this week's dip.
**What it might mean:** High body battery peak alongside low sleep score is unusual — it suggests body battery is charging well during the day but something is fragmenting sleep (common as running volume ramps for a new runner: DOMS, evening HR elevation, or novel training stress). This looks like accumulated load from the two heaviest training weeks of the entire log, landing as fatigue a few days later.
**What to watch:** Check bedtime HR/respiration on this week specifically — if it's elevated versus baseline, this is training-load-driven sleep disruption, not illness or dose-related, and argues for an easier week rather than pushing volume further.

## Protein threshold around 140g tracks with the muscle-mass inflection
**What the data shows:** Through mid-September, muscle mass hovers 106–108 lb with protein frequently in the 90–125g range (e.g., four weeks ago at 125g, three weeks ago at just 89g). From late last month onward, protein consistently clears 140g (20 days ago: 174g, 19 days ago: 159g, a week ago: 170g, six days ago: 167g) and muscle mass trend shifts up to a new band of 107.5–109.3 lb, with the single highest reading (109.3 lb) two weeks ago following a run of 137–147g days.
**What it might mean:** Creatine was already onboard since two months ago with no muscle-mass response until protein intake also rose — suggesting protein was the limiting factor, not the creatine itself. The two together may be doing more than either alone, especially with semaglutide suppressing overall intake.
**What to watch:** Hold protein at 140g+ on strength days specifically and see if muscle-mass readings on the following 1–2 days are disproportionately higher than on days following sub-120g intake.

## Weight loss is decelerating right as the dose increased, not accelerating
**What the data shows:** From two months ago to four weeks ago (0.5mg, 28 days), weight fell 170.8→169.0 lb, about 1.8 lb in 4 weeks. From four weeks ago to today (1mg, 33 days), weight fell 169.6→167.6, roughly 2.0 lb over a longer span — a similar or slightly slower rate despite the higher dose, even as workouts roughly doubled (3-4/week to 6-7/week at the peak).
**What it might mean:** Body recomposition (fat 28.0%→25.5%, muscle 107.0→108.6 lb) is happening instead of pure weight loss — scale weight is masking real progress. This is easy to misread as the dose "not working."
**What to watch:** Track body-fat% trend and waist/photos rather than scale weight alone when evaluating the 1mg dose's effectiveness.

## Hunger is creeping up, not down, as dose duration extends
**What the data shows:** Morning hunger rose from 4.2/10 (three weeks ago) to 5.0/10 (two weeks ago), the highest value logged, before dipping back to 4.0 (this week) — but that latest dip coincides with today's data showing only 301 kcal logged (a near-fast day), which would artificially suppress next-morning hunger readings or reflect a GI event rather than genuine appetite control.
**What it might mean:** The two-weeks-ago hunger spike sits one week into increased training volume (7 workouts the prior week) — exercise-driven appetite may be overriding semaglutide's suppression, a classic pattern as activity increases on GLP-1s. Today's near-zero intake day is an outlier worth flagging rather than averaging in.
**What to watch:** Compare morning hunger specifically on high-volume training weeks vs. rest weeks going forward — if hunger consistently tracks workout count rather than days-on-dose, it's activity-driven, not tolerance-driven.

## Workout volume doubled right when recovery metrics were at their best — then recovery paid for it
**What the data shows:** Readiness peaked at 83 four weeks ago and stayed strong (76, 75) through late last month, which preceded the jump to 7 workouts (three weeks ago) and 6 workouts (two weeks ago) — the two highest-volume weeks in the data. The very next week (this week), sleep score and readiness both dropped to their lowest or near-lowest points (65 and 66).
**What it might mean:** Good readiness scores likely gave implicit "green light" to push volume, but the ramp (3-4 workouts/week sustained for a month, then nearly doubled) outpaced recovery capacity by about a week's lag — classic new-runner overreach pattern layered onto existing cycling/lifting load.
**What to watch:** When readiness exceeds ~80, cap volume increases to +1-2 sessions rather than doubling, and treat the week-after as a deload check.

## Highest-confidence pattern
The lagged relationship between the two highest-volume training weeks (three weeks ago, two weeks ago) and the subsequent recovery collapse (sleep score 65, readiness 66 this week) is the strongest and most actionable signal in the dataset.

## Most worth testing
For the next two weeks, cap total workouts at 5/week and see whether sleep score and readiness in the following week stay above 75 — this would confirm volume (not dose or diet) is driving the recovery dips.

## Weight & Body Composition
Weight held essentially flat week over week (**168.3 lb avg, -0.1 lb**), continuing a plateau after the initial drop from semaglutide. Daily readings bounced between 167.7–169.2 lb, which is normal noise, not a stall signal yet — but worth watching over the next 1-2 weeks since this is now week 5 at the 1mg dose. With training volume increasing, some of this plateau could reflect muscle retention/gain offsetting fat loss, especially with creatine on board.

## Nutrition
A strong week: **7/7 days under calorie target, 7/7 days hitting protein goal, and 6/7 days hitting fiber** (only Tuesday fell short at 17g). No weekend drift — if anything, Thursday and Friday were the strongest protein days (170g, 167g). Calories stayed tight in a narrow 1539–1676 kcal band all week, showing good consistency rather than big swings. This is excellent adherence for someone on appetite-suppressing medication, where under-eating protein is the more common risk.

## Training
Solid, balanced week: two strength sessions (**Mon full body, Fri lower body**), one cycling ride, two run sessions (Thu beginner run, Sun walk+run), plus yoga. This lines up well with the 5K goal while preserving the two strength days. Running volume is still light (20 min sessions) — appropriate for a new runner building a base. Recovery metrics look healthy: **7.6h avg sleep, HRV 48ms, RHR 52bpm** — no signs of overreaching despite the mixed-modality load.

## Hunger & Symptoms
Morning hunger averaged a moderate **5.0/10**, consistent with appetite suppression working but not overly aggressive. No symptoms logged — no GI issues or soreness flags despite the increased training variety this week.

## One Thing Going Well
**Protein consistency** — hitting target every single day (even 170g on a lower-calorie day) while staying under calorie goals is a hard balance to strike, and it's being executed well.

## One Focus for Next Week
Nudge the two run sessions slightly longer (e.g., 20 → 25 min) or add a third short run, since 5K prep benefits from gradually increasing time-on-feet — current volume is safe but will need to build if a race is approaching.

## Weight & Body Composition
Weight continued its gradual downward drift: **168.3 lb avg, down 0.5 lb from last week's 168.8 lb**. Daily readings bounced between 168.0–168.9 lb, which is normal noise, not a plateau. This is consistent, controlled loss — four weeks into 1mg semaglutide, the trend line is doing exactly what's expected.

## Nutrition
Calories were well-controlled — **5/5 logged days came in at or under the 1650 kcal target**, including two days notably low (1229 and 1286 kcal) that may reflect strong appetite suppression rather than deliberate restriction. Protein is the weak spot: only **2/5 days hit 90%+ of the 140g target**, with Thursday (114g) and especially the weekend's start (109g on Sunday) falling short. Fiber is similarly inconsistent — just **2/5 days above 85% of the 25g target**, with Thursday dipping to 19g. Friday and Saturday have no logs at all, so the real adherence picture may be incomplete. Saturday-adjacent data (the 26th) shows the week's best fiber (34g) and decent protein, suggesting weekend meals aren't necessarily worse — just less consistently logged.

## Training
A full week: two runs (20 min each), two strength sessions, one cycling ride, one yoga session, and a longer walk/run — seven sessions total, directly supporting the 5K-prep-plus-two-strength-days focus. This is well-aligned with stated goals, and the balance between running volume and strength maintenance looks sustainable for a new runner avoiding overuse issues. Recovery metrics support the load: **8.0h avg sleep, HRV 45ms, RHR 59bpm** — all solid, no signs of overreaching.

## Hunger & Symptoms
Morning hunger averaged **4.2/10** — moderate and manageable, consistent with appetite suppression from semaglutide without signs of excessive restriction. No symptoms logged, which combined with good sleep and HRV suggests the current training and medication load is being tolerated well.

## One Thing Going Well
**Training consistency is excellent** — seven sessions spanning running, strength, cycling, and yoga in one week, hitting both the 5K-build and strength-maintenance goals simultaneously.

## One Focus for Next Week
**Prioritize protein on run days** — Tuesday, Thursday, and Sunday (the lower-protein days) line up with running sessions; add a protein-forward snack or shake post-run to close the gap toward 140g, which will support recovery and preserve lean mass while in a calorie deficit.

## Weight & Body Composition
Weight held essentially flat week-over-week (168.8 lb avg vs. 168.9 lb prior, **-0.1 lb**), with daily readings bouncing between 168.3-169.3 lb. This is a plateau week, not a concern — you're 3 weeks into the 1mg semaglutide dose, and some stabilization after earlier losses is normal. Nothing here suggests a problem, but worth watching if the flat trend continues into next week.

## Nutrition
Calories were well controlled — **7/7 days under target**, including a notably low 1091 kcal on Sunday. Protein was inconsistent: strong on Tuesday-Thursday (147-174g, all above target) but fell short early week (89-121g on Sunday/Monday), landing at **4/7 days hitting the 140g goal**. Fiber followed a similar pattern — solid mid-week (22-23g) but Sunday's 11g was a notable gap. The second half of the week (Tue-Thu) was your strongest stretch for both protein and fiber; the weekend start was the weak point, likely tied to lower overall intake those days.

## Training
Four sessions logged: one cycling ride (45 min, 477 kcal), two short run sessions (15 min and a 20 min walk/run), and one restorative yoga block. This fits your 5K-prep phase — low-volume, easy running mixed with cycling as your aerobic base. **No strength sessions logged this week**, which breaks from your stated two-day lifting goal. Recovery metrics look healthy (7.2h sleep, 48ms HRV, 56bpm RHR) and would support adding a lifting day without issue.

## Hunger & Symptoms
No hunger or symptom data logged this week — worth tracking morning hunger at least a few days to see how the dose increase is affecting appetite, especially given the very low Sunday calorie day.

## One Thing Going Well
**Perfect calorie adherence** (7/7 days at or under target) while still fitting in four workouts — strong discipline without obvious energy crashes in training logs.

## One Focus for Next Week
**Get both strength sessions back on the calendar** — none were logged this week despite good recovery numbers supporting it. Pair this with hitting protein target on run/rest days (Sun/Mon were the gaps) to support lifting performance and preserve lean mass while losing weight.
